slides.heading: Design a Code-Deployment System
slides.subtitle: SystemsExpert design walkthrough
slides.narration: In this lecture we design a Code-Deployment System. We'll follow the interview framework: clarify, set requirements, estimate, sketch the architecture, define the data and API, then dive into the hard parts and the trade-offs.

slides.heading: Clarifying questions
bullets: Build + deploy, or deploy only?
How many machines/regions; how big are binaries?
How fast must a deploy reach every machine?
Do we need rollbacks and canary/gradual rollouts?
slides.narration: Start by clarifying the scope with your interviewer. Good questions here are: Build plus deploy, or deploy only? How many machines or regions; how big are binaries? How fast must a deploy reach every machine? Do we need rollbacks and canary or gradual rollouts?

slides.heading: Functional requirements
bullets: Trigger a build for a commit SHA
Store build artifacts
Deploy a chosen build to all hosts (global) with progress
Roll back to a previous build
slides.narration: The functional requirements. Trigger a build for a commit SHA. Store build artifacts. Deploy a chosen build to all hosts (global) with progress. Roll back to a previous build.

slides.heading: Non-functional requirements
bullets: Builds take minutes but must never be lost or run twice
Deploy to hundreds of thousands of hosts in < ~30 min
Highly available control plane
slides.narration: The non-functional requirements. Builds take minutes but must never be lost or run twice. Deploy to hundreds of thousands of hosts in under about 30 min. Highly available control plane.

slides.heading: Capacity estimates
bullets: ~thousands of builds/day; artifacts up to ~10 GB
~100k-1M hosts across ~10 regions
Fan-out: 10 GB x 1M hosts is impossible from one store -> regional replication + peer-to-peer distribution
slides.narration: Now some rough capacity estimates, which drive the design. about thousands of builds per day; artifacts up to about 10 GB. about 100k-1M hosts across about 10 regions. Fan-out: 10 GB x 1M hosts is impossible from one store to regional replication plus peer-to-peer distribution.

slides.heading: Capacity: worked out
bullets: Artifact 10 GB × 100k hosts = 1 PB of transfer
One store at 100 Gbps ≈ 12.5 GB/s → ~22 hours
10 regions + P2P: bandwidth grows with hosts
Goal: whole fleet in < 30 min
slides.narration: Let's actually work the numbers. A ten gigabyte artifact sent to a hundred thousand hosts is a petabyte of transfer. Even one store pushing a hundred gigabits a second would need about twenty-two hours. With regional replicas and peer-to-peer sharing, every host also uploads, so total bandwidth scales with the fleet. That's how we get the whole fleet updated in under thirty minutes.

slides.heading: High-level architecture
edges: Goal state: desired build per service
Goal state: desired build per service
slides.narration: Here's the high-level architecture. Engineer / CI trigger connects to Deploy API. Deploy API connects to Jobs table: SQL queue and Goal state: desired build per service. Jobs table: SQL queue connects to Build workers. Build workers connects to Global blob store. Global blob store connects to Regional blob replicas. Regional blob replicas connects to Peer-to-peer distribution in each region. Hosts' agents connects to Goal state: desired build per service and Peer-to-peer distribution in each region.

slides.heading: Data model
bullets: jobs(id, sha, status{QUEUED,RUNNING,SUCCEEDED,FAILED}, worker_id, heartbeat_at, created_at)
builds(sha, artifact_url, size, checksum, regions_replicated[])
deployments(id, service, sha, strategy, status, started_at)
goal_state key/value: service -> sha (strongly consistent store, e.g. etcd/ZooKeeper)
slides.narration: Here is the data model. The jobs record holds id, sha, status QUEUED,RUNNING,SUCCEEDED,FAILED , worker id, heartbeat at, created at. The builds record holds sha, artifact url, size, checksum, regions replicated . The deployments record holds id, service, sha, strategy, status, started at. goal state key or value: service to sha (strongly consistent store, for example etcd or ZooKeeper).

slides.heading: API
slides.narration: The API. The main endpoints are: POST builds; GET builds by sha; POST deployments; GET deployments by id; POST deployments by id rollback. Each one is small, resource-oriented and easy to version.

slides.heading: Queue as a SQL table
bullets: Workers dequeue with UPDATE … SET status='RUNNING', worker_id=?
WHERE id=(SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED).
ACID guarantees each job runs once.
Workers heartbeat; a reaper resets stale RUNNING jobs.
slides.narration: Deep dive: the build queue is just a SQL table. A worker claims a job by updating its status to running inside a transaction, selecting the next queued row with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so two workers can never grab the same job. Workers send heartbeats, and a reaper resets any running job whose heartbeat goes stale.

slides.heading: Artifact distribution
bullets: Build writes to a global store, async replicated to regional stores; deploy only proceeds once all target regions have the artifact.
Within a region hosts fetch pieces from each other (BitTorrent-like) to avoid hot-spotting.
slides.narration: Deep dive: Artifact distribution. Build writes to a global store, async replicated to regional stores; deploy only proceeds once all target regions have the artifact. Within a region hosts fetch pieces from each other (BitTorrent-like) to avoid hot-spotting.

slides.heading: Goal state
bullets: Deploy just flips the desired sha in a consistent KV store; host agents watch it, download, swap, and report health.
Rollback = set goal to previous sha.
slides.narration: Deep dive: Goal state. Deploy just flips the desired sha in a consistent KV store; host agents watch it, download, swap, and report health. Rollback equals set goal to previous sha.

slides.heading: Key decisions
bullets: SQL table as the build queue → exactly-once claims via row locks
Goal state, not push commands → idempotent, easy rollback
Regional replicas + P2P → removes the bandwidth bottleneck
Canary stages → limits blast radius
slides.narration: Let's pull together the key decisions. SQL table as the build queue, because exactly-once claims via row locks. Goal state, not push commands, because idempotent, easy rollback. Regional replicas plus P2P, because removes the bandwidth bottleneck. Canary stages, because limits blast radius.

slides.heading: Trade-offs & alternatives
bullets: SQL queue vs Kafka: SQL gives exactly-once claim semantics with modest throughput, which is enough
P2P adds complexity but removes a bandwidth bottleneck
Canary stages slow deploys down but limit blast radius
slides.narration: Finally, the key trade-offs. SQL queue versus Kafka: SQL gives exactly-once claim semantics with modest throughput, which is enough. P2P adds complexity but removes a bandwidth bottleneck. Canary stages slow deploys down but limit blast radius.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Clarify scope, then functional + non-functional needs
Estimate load to size storage and fan-out
Core pieces: Engineer / CI trigger, Deploy API, Jobs table, Build workers, Global blob store
Know your trade-offs and failure modes
slides.narration: To recap a Code-Deployment System: we clarified the scope, set functional and non-functional requirements, estimated the load, sketched an architecture built around Engineer / CI trigger, Deploy API, Jobs table, Build workers, and walked through the deep dives and trade-offs. Practise explaining each decision out loud.
